Will Endley

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
the first television interview with Col Will Endley after he's released from death row in South Sudan.
Will is well spoken, has an unfortunate moustache and should work well on camera.
The idea is to get his sister Charmaine to expound on the anxiety, fear and hopeless sense of loss that Endley’s incarceration brought upon her. Her own career and family suffered immensely during the last few years. The story will be filmed in Cape Town Will Endley wrote some poetry during his incarceration. During my tenure at the NSS and later at the JCP, my future and prospects were very bleak. I composed a poem and left it with a friend for safekeeping and, if need be, to send it to my sister.

Summary:
William Endley is a 56 year old retired SANDF colonel. He was sentenced to death in February 2018 and suddenly set free in November 2018 as part of a peace deal between warring factions in South Sudan.
After his retirement from the SANDF he was involved with mine clearing operations in Iraq.
Endley was employed as an advisor in South Sudan in 2015. Because of his experience in integrating non statutory forces in the post 1994 South African National Defence Force, Endley was an ideal advisor to then deputy president, Dr Riek Machar. South Sudan has been mired in conflict for decades, Machar is a leader of the SPLM (Sudan Peoples Liberation Movement) he was appointed deputy president after the Compromise Peace Deal. It was at this time that Endley started working in South Sudan.
The peace agreement did not last and it didn’t take long for hostilities to flare up again. President Salva Kiir accused Machar of plotting to overthrow his government. Machar fled to South Africa where he is still under “house arrest”, Will Endley and others were arrested and detained.
For two years Endley was kept in horrific conditions. He was basically left to die.
Endley’s sister Charmaine initiated a campaign to free her brother.
It took two years for Endley to get his day in court. He was found guilty. A charge of attempting to overthrow the government, led to a sentence of death by hanging. Shocked family and friends resorted to petitioning government. Then, unexpectedly a peace agreement was signed by the warring factions in South Sudan and president Kiir ordered that Will Endley should be released, within days he was back in South Africa. Will Endley is a father, grandfather and sees himself as a peacekeeper, it just happened that he found himself on the wrong side. He’s presently in Cape Town where he is contemplating the future that he did not have two weeks ago.

Further information:
FAREWELL Trained and selected to lead from the front,
I lived by the sword which has never been blunt.
Planning,leading,training has been my lot,
Facing the enemy - shot after shot!
Academically trained and the univarsity of life,
Ideal background for martial struggle and strife.
Death is the conqueror but victory is there,
Selfdoubt at times lays one soul bare.
Betrayed and captured at a loss for words,
To be eaten by worms and turned into turds.
Was it worth it to have it end in this place?
Questions abound,harsh reality to face.
The glamour of risk is not what people may think,
The many war heroes abound only in comfort and drink.
Stand by your principles to the very brutal end,
Knowing you will face it without a friend.
As the sun goes down you can remember me,
If we wronged each other please let it be.
In the great unknown we will meet again,
Without uncertainty,anguish,tears or pain.

Press Release:


Home for Christmas: Colonel Will Endley
Retired SANDF Colonel William Endley waited two years for his day in court. A military advisor on the wrong side of the war in South Sudan, Endley was found guilty of attempting to overthrow the government and was sentenced to death by hanging. He was preparing himself for death when a presidential pardon as part of the South Sudanese peace process earlier this month secured his release. Carte Blanche recounts what the ordeal has cost Endley and his family.
Producers: Efpé Senekal
Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


Will Endley South Sudan Script 23-11-2018
Alive and a free man, retired South African National Defence Force colonel William Endley is finally back home. Since 2016 Endley had spent two years behind bars in a South Sudanese prison, before being sentenced to death by hanging in February this year. It was pure grit and resilience that made him hang on for all these months on death row.
WILL ENDLEY: I managed to pull through, there were a couple of times I didn’t think I was going to make it. The late major Mabiile who was himself shot by unknown gunmen a few weeks later, he was called, he said no the Khawaja, or the white man is dying. And he said:”Simple, just let him die…” . And when I heard this, I felt stubborn, hardegat, and I just said:”There’s no way I’m going to die on this floor…”.
But Endley was suddenly set free this month as part of a peace deal between warring factions in South Sudan.
The country is landlocked between the Central African Republic and Ethiopia. In 2011 it became the newest country on the continent when an overwhelming majority voted “yes” for independence from Sudan in a referendum. Ebrahim Deen of the Afro Middle East Centre makes a study of Sudan
EBRAHIM DEEN: Prior to the state’s formation, we must know that there was conflict between the regions in the north and South of Sudan…a very violent conflict, and a conflict that led in 2005 to the signing of the comprehensive peace agreement which was the CPA, steered or largely engineered by by Omar Al Bashir and than SPLM leader John Garang – Garan’s death later meant that Rick Machar became vice president and Salva Kiir became the president of the SPLMhe SPLM…the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement
Deputy president Rick Machar employed Endley as a consultant.
WILL ENDLEY: and he asked me to become his senior security advisor. Specifically looking at integration, also the security assessment which was part of the peace deal. At that point I assisted him during the negotiation process, specifically advising him on security aspects.
Endley was perfectly qualified for the job. He was born a soldier.
WILL ENDLEY: Grandfather from my mother’s side was in the special service battalion in the second world war, so from a very young age, all I was interested in , was to become a soldier. So I think I was about five years old when I decided to become a dumb PF, as I call it.
Endley joined the army as a PF, or Permanent Force member. He left the SANDF after a successful career, with the rank of colonel. The colonel now entered the world of military and security contractors, sometimes seen as mercenaries.
WILL ENDLEY: You know the word, mercenary, is very relative and loosely thrown around. At times it becomes insulting. Many South Africans in Iraq and other countries were doing humanitarian de-mining, as I was in Iraq, and at the same time were doing security work . But mercenaries actually physically fighting, that never took place.
In 2004, Endley commenced his career in the private sector.
WILL ENDLEY: I remained in Iraq for three years, I then was transferred to South Sudan as liaison officer for Ronce De-mining, we had contracts with the World Food Program, to specifically clear roads for them. At that point Sudan was one country, I was given the Order of Merit by president Omar Al Bashir, for the work that I did there
After his stint in Sudan, Endley became the country manager for Ronco Group in Afghanistan, Three years later, he was back in South Sudan.
WILL ENDLEY: At that point doctor Riek Machar was vice president of South Sudan. At the same time we became very good personal friends. Which we still are. Things were going very well and all of a sudden, the war broke out.
EBRAHIM DEEN: The transitional constitution gave most of the power in the Presidency and Salva Kiir, basically was using this power to actually autocratically dictate situations and remove governors, political officials and there was a conflict within the SPLM between him and Machar which soon militarised and it turned into armed conflict and because Kiir and Machar were part of, or represented different ethnicities, or ethnic groupings, the Dinka and Nuer. We started seeinf this conflict become ethnisized.
Endley remained in South Sudan even after the RMA group closed their operations in 2014. He met up with Machar again.
They left for South Sudan under the Auspices of the United Nations, to take part in the peace process.
EBRAHIM DEEN: In 2015 a peace deal was signed. It was more a power sharing
Kiir accused Machar of trying to overthrow his government. It was war.
ENDLEY: the fighting broke out, …a few hundred …about 08h30 in the morning, helicopter gunships, tanks, artillery – an infantry assault took place, specifically to push back onto doctor Machar’s residence…and the plan was, I believe to kill him. Doctor Machar himself was wounded when he escaped to the DRC. He then came to South Africa where he was kept in house arrest for 2 years. I remained behind, there were people from the movement still there with me. I noticed a lot of national security people moving around , in uniform. Everytime I went somewhere, I was followed. That night I was arrested. They say I was hiding in the hotel, I was not hiding in the hotel, I was having a cold beer in the bar I was then taken to the National Security Centre, in Jebo, no one was allowed to talk to me.
Meanwhile in South Africa Endley’s family hadn’t heard from him in weeks. It was highly unusual.
UPS CHARMAINE: There’s 20 months between William and I, so we grew up close– his military career took him all over the country but we always kept close contact with each other. Basically my instinct, my brother was in trouble, something I always thought could happen. It was just sort of a natural thing for me to take the lead and set up contacts as I could.
Endley’s sister Charmaine initiated a campaign to free her brother.
CHARMAINE: There was no proof that he was alive, I had to pay dollars to access the first photo which I got which was very heart breaking and shocking because he was very ill.
Malnourished, and isolated…Endley was left to die.

CHARMAINE: And the not knowing if he was dead or alive and what he’s actually going through. For the first few months that was the worst.
ENDLEY: For a few weeks I was in a daze. I think that is when some of the first photographs were taken as well. I remember talking on a telephone to my sister and at that point I thought it was a dream. I didn’t know if it happened or not.
It took two years for Endley to get his day in court. He was found guilty of espionage and attempting to overthrow the government and was sentenced to 9 years on lesser charges including entering South Sudan illegally and bringing in arms. He was sentenced to death by hanging for treason.
ENDLEY: I realised,day for day, let the sun rise, let the sun set. If it’s a good day, it’s a good day, if it’s a bad day, it’s a bad day. But I could not think about tomorrow , I cannot think about yesterday. What am I doing here? And I started composing poems, things in my mind… this is what kept me going
Then, unexpectedly a peace agreement was signed by the warring factions in South Sudan and president Kiir ordered Endleys release.
CHARMAINE ENDLEY WALKER : My phone rang and she said to me: ‘William is coming home… That was the moment, that we all waited for
Will Endley: At one point I hated the people, slapping us around, beating people, whatever. Then I realised that by allowing them to control my life, I’m allowing them to win, so I have to stand back, accept them for what they are, and make sure I’m not the same
